tagline: Paul's last letter, written from a Roman prison as he faces death, urging Timothy to guard the gospel, endure suffering, and hand the faith on.
overview:
Second Timothy is the most personal of the Pastoral Letters and, if Paul wrote it, the last letter we have from him. He is in chains in Rome, many of his companions have left him, his first hearing has gone badly, and he expects to die. He writes to Timothy, his beloved child in the faith, to call him to courage: not to be ashamed of the gospel or of Paul the prisoner, to fan into flame the gift God gave him, to share in suffering like a good soldier, and to entrust the teaching to faithful people who will teach others.

The letter looks both backward and forward. It looks back on a life spent for the gospel, from Paul's persecutions in Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra to his final confession that he has fought the good fight, finished the race, and kept the faith (4:7). And it looks forward to hard times in which people will turn from sound teaching to myths, and to the day when the Lord, the righteous Judge, will give the crown of righteousness to all who have longed for his appearing. Between these, it holds Timothy to Scripture, which is God-breathed and able to make a person wise for salvation.

Few letters in the New Testament carry so much feeling. Paul remembers Timothy's tears, longs to see him, asks him to come before winter and bring his cloak and his books, and names both those who deserted him and those who stood by him. It is a letter about passing on a faith that costs something, written by someone paying the cost.
author:
The letter names Paul as its author (1:1) and is full of personal detail: the names of Timothy's grandmother and mother (1:5), friends and deserters by name, the cloak left at Troas, and the request for scrolls and parchments (4:13). The early church accepted it as Paul's without dispute, and it is listed with the other Pastoral Letters in the Muratorian list of the late second century.

The authorship debate over the Pastoral Letters applies here too (see the introduction to 1 Timothy). Scholars who think a later follower of Paul wrote all three point to their shared vocabulary and style, which differ from Paul's undisputed letters, and to features they see as reflecting a later period. On this view the letter is a farewell testament written in Paul's name, a recognized ancient form in which a great figure's last words are set down for later generations. Scholars who hold that Paul wrote it answer that the many personal details are hard to explain as invention, since they serve no obvious purpose for a later writer, and that the style suits a private letter to a close coworker written under very different conditions from Paul's letters to churches.

Some scholars treat 2 Timothy separately from 1 Timothy and Titus, judging that its personal character makes Pauline authorship more likely for it than for the other two. Mediating views suggest that Paul, imprisoned and perhaps unable to write freely, relied heavily on a secretary (Luke, the only one with him according to 4:11, is often proposed), or that genuine notes from Paul were worked into the letter by a later editor. Evangelical scholarship generally holds to Paul's authorship; many critical scholars do not, though a significant number regard 2 Timothy as the Pastoral Letter with the strongest claim.
date: If Paul wrote the letter, it most likely comes from his final imprisonment in Rome, shortly before his execution under the emperor Nero, who died in AD 68. Early Christian tradition, reported by Eusebius in the fourth century, holds that Paul was released from the house arrest described at the end of Acts and later arrested again and put to death in Rome. On that view the letter dates to about AD 64 to 67. A minority of scholars place it during an earlier imprisonment, such as the one in Rome at the end of Acts or in Caesarea, but the letter's expectation of imminent death and its travel notes fit a later setting more easily. Scholars who regard the letter as written by a later follower usually date it between about AD 80 and 110.
setting:
Paul is a prisoner in Rome (1:8, 16-17; 2:9), not in the relatively open house arrest of Acts 28, where he received visitors freely, but in harsher chains: Onesiphorus had to search diligently to find him. He has already had a first hearing, at which no one stood with him (4:16). If the traditional dating is right, this imprisonment falls after the great fire of Rome in AD 64, when, according to the Roman historian Tacitus, Nero blamed the Christians and put many to death in brutal ways. To be associated with a Christian prisoner in that climate was dangerous, which helps explain why many had deserted Paul and why he urges Timothy not to be ashamed.

Timothy seems to be in or near Ephesus: the letter greets the household of Onesiphorus, who had served in Ephesus, and mentions Hymenaeus, the false teacher named in 1 Timothy 1:20. Paul asks him to come to Rome quickly, before winter closed the sea lanes, and to bring Mark. Timothy is still facing the false teachers described in 1 Timothy, now even more persuasive, and he must carry on without Paul.
purpose: Paul writes to strengthen Timothy for faithful ministry after Paul is gone. He urges him to guard the good deposit of the gospel, to suffer for it without shame, to teach it accurately and hand it on to reliable people, to correct opponents gently, to continue in the Scriptures, and to preach the word whatever the response. He also writes for practical reasons: he wants Timothy to come to him soon, bringing Mark, his cloak, and his books. Behind the letter lies a concern for the next generation of the church, since the apostle who founded so many churches is about to die.
story: Second Timothy stands at the end of Paul's story as the New Testament presents it. Acts ends with Paul in Rome preaching the kingdom of God unhindered; this letter shows what may lie beyond Acts, with Paul in chains, about to be poured out like a drink offering. It is the moment when the apostolic generation hands the faith to those who come after, and it connects Paul's mission to the ongoing life of the church. In the order of the New Testament it follows 1 Timothy and is followed by Titus and Philemon.
christ: The letter's gospel is summed up in the command to remember Jesus Christ, raised from the dead, descended from David (2:8). Christ Jesus has abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel (1:10). God's grace was given in him before time began. He is the faithful one who remains faithful even when his people are faithless (2:13), the Lord who stood by Paul when everyone else deserted him (4:17), and the righteous Judge who will judge the living and the dead at his appearing (4:1, 8). Paul's suffering is shaped by Christ's: those who die with him will live with him, and those who endure will reign with him.
reading: Read 2 Timothy as a farewell letter, a genre with deep roots in Scripture and Jewish tradition (compare Moses in Deuteronomy, Joshua 23-24, and Paul's own farewell in Acts 20). A departing leader recalls his life, warns of dangers ahead, charges his successor, and entrusts the future to God. Watch for the words of shame and not being ashamed, of guarding and entrusting, and of suffering and endurance. The passage on Scripture in 3:16-17 is best read in its setting: Paul is not writing a doctrinal essay on the Bible but telling Timothy why the Scriptures he has known since childhood are sufficient for his task. Do not skip the list of names in chapter 4; they show that Paul's ministry was always a team, and that desertion and loyalty had names.

structure.title: Do not be ashamed
structure.summary: Paul thanks God for Timothy's faith, urges him to fan into flame his gift and share in suffering for the gospel, and contrasts those who deserted him with the loyal Onesiphorus.

structure.title: Be strong and entrust the teaching
structure.summary: Using images of soldier, athlete, farmer, and workman, Paul calls Timothy to endure, remember the risen Christ, handle the word accurately, and correct opponents gently.

structure.title: Hard times and the sufficiency of Scripture
structure.summary: Paul describes the corrupt people of the last days, points to his own example of persecution, and grounds Timothy in the God-breathed Scriptures.

structure.title: Preach the word; the last words of Paul
structure.summary: A solemn charge to preach, Paul's confidence that he has finished his race, and personal requests and greetings as he faces death.

themes.title: Suffering without shame
themes.body: Paul is a prisoner, and to be linked to him is costly. Again and again he urges Timothy not to be ashamed and to join him in suffering (1:8; 2:3). Suffering for the gospel is not a sign of failure but the expected path of those who want to live godly lives in Christ Jesus (3:12), and it is endured by the power of God, not by grit.

themes.title: Guarding and handing on the gospel
themes.body: The gospel is a treasure entrusted to Timothy, to be guarded with the help of the Holy Spirit (1:14) and passed on to faithful people who will teach others (2:2). The letter pictures four generations of faith: Paul, Timothy, faithful men, and others. Tradition in this sense is not dead habit but living testimony carried from one person to the next.

themes.title: Scripture
themes.body: Timothy has known the Holy Scriptures from infancy, and they can make him wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus (3:15). All Scripture is God-breathed and equips the servant of God for every good work (3:16-17). This is the New Testament's most direct statement about the nature of Scripture, and it undergirds the charge to preach the word (4:2).

themes.title: Faithfulness to the end
themes.body: The letter is written by someone who has kept the faith and now looks to the crown laid up for him (4:7-8). God is faithful even when we are not (2:13), and the Lord will rescue Paul and bring him safely into his heavenly kingdom (4:18). Endurance is sustained by confidence in God's faithfulness and in the day of Christ's appearing.

keyChapters.why: Sets the letter's tone of courage and grace, with a rich summary of salvation by God's purpose and grace given in Christ before time began.
Calls Timothy to hand on the teaching, remember the risen Christ, and correct opponents with gentleness, and contains an early Christian saying about dying and reigning with Christ.
Contains the New Testament's central statement on the inspiration and usefulness of Scripture.
Paul's final charge to preach the word and his farewell: he has fought the good fight, finished the race, and kept the faith.
